claim: PRC1 was depleted 90 ± 2% by siRNA before addition of opto-PRC1.
source: Endogenous PRC1 was depleted 90 ± 2% (all results are mean ± s.e.m.) by siRNA before addition of opto-PRC1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript reports a specific measurement of PRC1 depletion efficiency with quantitative data (90 ± 2%) and references a figure showing the experimental result.

claim: The length of PRC1 streaks in opto cells before exposure to blue light was 3.77 ± 0.08 µm.
source: Before exposure to the blue light, opto-PRC1 had normal localization on the microtubule bundles in the spindle midzone (Figure 1B; 0:00 min), with the length of PRC1 streaks of 3.77 ± 0.08 µm (n = 193 bundles, N = 30 cells), consistent with that of endogenous and fluorescently labeled PRC1 in metaphase (Kajtez et al., 2016; Polak et al., 2017)
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative measurements of PRC1 streak length with sample size and compares to published data.

claim: Addition of opto-PRC1 did not change the duration of metaphase.
source: Addition of opto-PRC1 did not change the duration of metaphase, as inferred from the fraction of cells that entered anaphase during image acquisition, which was similar in cells with endogenous PRC1 and cells treated with PRC1 siRNA and containing opto-PRC1 (79 ± 6%, N = 37, and 71 ± 5%, N = 72, respectively; p = 0.4, Pearson's Chi-squared test; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative data comparing anaphase entry rates between conditions with statistical analysis.

claim: 88 ± 3% of opto-PRC1 was removed after 20 min of exposure to blue light with a half-time of 4.2 ± 0.1 min.
source: We found that 88 ± 3% of opto-PRC1 was removed after 20 min of exposure to the blue light with a half-time of 4.2 ± 0.1 min (Figure 1C).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative measurements of PRC1 removal kinetics with reference to a figure showing the data.

claim: After the blue light was switched off, opto-PRC1 signal restored to 65 ± 1% of the initial intensity within 10 min, with return half-time being 0.71 ± 0.04 min.
source: After the blue light was switched off, opto-PRC1 signal restored to 65 ± 1% of the initial intensity within 10 min, with return half-time being 0.71 ± 0.04 min (Figure 1C).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative measurements of PRC1 return kinetics with reference to a figure.

claim: The faster PRC1 return to the spindle in comparison with its removal may be due to the higher affinity difference between PRC1 binding to the spindle and to the membrane in the dark than under light.
source: The faster PRC1 return to the spindle in comparison with its removal may be due to the higher affinity difference between PRC1 binding to the spindle and to the membrane in the dark than under light.
evidence: The manuscript proposes a mechanistic explanation for observed kinetic differences based on binding affinity.

claim: PRC1 has a life-time of several seconds on single microtubules and a 10-fold preference for overlap regions in vitro.
source: This result is consistent with PRC1 having a life-time of several seconds on single microtubules and a 10-fold preference for overlap regions in vitro (Subramanian et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites published in vitro data about PRC1 binding properties.

claim: Acute removal of opto-PRC1 resulted in movement of sister kinetochore pairs away from the metaphase plate.
source: Surprisingly, we observed that the acute removal of opto-PRC1 resulted in movement of sister kinetochore pairs away from the metaphase plate (Figure 2B; Figure 2—video 1)
evidence: The manuscript reports an observed phenotype with reference to figures and videos showing the data.

claim: Upon opto-PRC1 removal, the distances of sister kinetochore midpoints from the equatorial plane increased.
source: Upon opto-PRC1 removal, the distances of sister kinetochore midpoints from the equatorial plane increased (dEQ, Figure 2B,C,D; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative measurements of kinetochore positioning with reference to figures.

claim: While >95% of kinetochore pairs were found within the region of PRC1 streaks before removal of opto-PRC1, 9.3 ± 2.7% of kinetochore pairs made excursions far outside this region after opto-PRC1 removal.
source: While >95% of kinetochore pairs were found within the region of PRC1 streaks, that is, less than 2 µm away from the equatorial plane before removal of opto-PRC1, 9.3 ± 2.7% of kinetochore pairs made excursions far outside this region after opto-PRC1 removal (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative data comparing kinetochore positioning before and after PRC1 removal.

claim: The displaced kinetochores were found more often in the inner part of the spindle than in the outer regions.
source: The displaced kinetochores were found more often in the inner part of the spindle, that is, close to the long spindle axis, than in the outer regions (Figure 2E).
evidence: The manuscript reports spatial distribution of displaced kinetochores with reference to a figure.

claim: Displaced kinetochores upon opto-PRC1 removal had lower inter-kinetochore distance in comparison to non-displaced ones.
source: These displaced kinetochores upon opto-PRC1 removal had lower inter-kinetochore distance in comparison to non-displaced ones, suggesting that kinetochore displacement was related to a more severe reduction of tension (Figure 2F).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative measurements comparing inter-kinetochore distances between displaced and non-displaced kinetochores.

claim: Kinetochores remained displaced even after opto-PRC1 return.
source: On average, kinetochores remained displaced even after opto-PRC1 return (Figure 2D).
evidence: The manuscript reports persistent kinetochore displacement after PRC1 return with reference to a figure.

claim: PRC1 has a role in keeping kinetochores in tight alignment on the metaphase plate.
source: We conclude that PRC1 has a role in keeping kinetochores in tight alignment on the metaphase plate.
evidence: The manuscript draws a conclusion based on the observed effects of PRC1 removal on kinetochore alignment.

claim: The mean inter-kinetochore distance was reduced when opto-PRC1 was removed.
source: The mean inter-kinetochore distance (dKC, Figure 2C) was reduced when opto-PRC1 was removed (Figure 2G; Figure 2—figure supplement 1D)
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative measurements of inter-kinetochore distance changes upon PRC1 removal.

claim: The inter-kinetochore distance after 20 min of exposure to blue light (0.79 ± 0.01 µm) was closer to metaphase (0.87 ± 0.01 µm) than prometaphase (0.66 ± 0.01 µm) values.
source: and the distance after 20 min of exposure to the blue light (0.79 ± 0.01 µm) was closer to metaphase (0.87 ± 0.01 µm) than prometaphase (0.66 ± 0.01 µm) values (see Materials and methods), suggesting that tension was not completely lost and that these changes were not due to kinetochore detachment from k-fibers (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative measurements comparing inter-kinetochore distances across different conditions and cell cycle stages.

claim: The fraction of cells that entered anaphase during image acquisition was similar in control and opto cells.
source: In agreement with this, the fraction of cells that entered anaphase during image acquisition was similar in control and opto cells (71 ± 5%, N = 72, and 60 ± 5%, N = 93, respectively; p = 0.1, Pearson's Chi-squared test; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), indicating that PRC1 removal did not prevent spindle assembly checkpoint satisfaction.
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative data comparing anaphase entry rates with statistical analysis.

claim: After opto-PRC1 return to the spindle, inter-kinetochore distance increased, implying restoration of tension, although not to the original value.
source: After opto-PRC1 return to the spindle, inter-kinetochore distance increased, implying restoration of tension, although not to the original value (Figure 2G).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative measurements of inter-kinetochore distance after PRC1 return.

claim: Removal of opto-PRC1 caused misorientation of sister kinetochores.
source: We observed that removal of opto-PRC1 caused misorientation of sister kinetochores, that is, increased αKC (Figure 2B,H; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,E).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative measurements of kinetochore orientation changes upon PRC1 removal.

claim: Misoriented kinetochores were found at a larger distance from the equatorial plane and closer to the long spindle axis.
source: Misoriented kinetochores were found at a larger distance from the equatorial plane and closer to the long spindle axis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The manuscript reports spatial distribution of misoriented kinetochores with reference to a figure.

claim: Sister kinetochore pairs remained misoriented even after opto-PRC1 return.
source: Interestingly, sister kinetochore pairs remained misoriented even after opto-PRC1 return (Figure 2H).
evidence: The manuscript reports persistent kinetochore misorientation after PRC1 return with reference to a figure.

claim: PRC1 bundles were misoriented upon PRC1 return.
source: Similarly, PRC1 bundles were misoriented upon PRC1 return (see Materials and methods, Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: The manuscript reports measurements of PRC1 bundle orientation with reference to methods and a figure.

claim: When PRC1 returns to the overlaps whose geometry was perturbed by PRC1 removal, it likely confines the chromosomes in new positions and orientations.
source: These results suggest that when PRC1 returns to the overlaps whose geometry was perturbed by PRC1 removal, it likely confines the chromosomes in new positions and orientations.
evidence: The manuscript proposes a mechanistic explanation for observed persistent misorientation based on PRC1 binding to perturbed overlaps.

claim: The observed effects of PRC1 removal on inter-kinetochore distance, kinetochore alignment and orientation did not change when SiR-tubulin was added.
source: The observed effects of PRC1 removal on inter-kinetochore distance, kinetochore alignment and orientation did not change when SiR-tubulin was added (dKC p = 0.82, dEQ p = 0.27, αKC p = 0.61, respectively; t-test).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical comparisons showing no significant differences with SiR-tubulin addition.

claim: The effects of PRC1 removal were found neither in control experiments in cells without iLID nor in cells expressing only CENP-A-GFP without SiR-tubulin imaged with the same illumination protocol.
source: The effects of PRC1 removal were found neither in control experiments in cells without iLID, which were stained with SiR-tubulin, nor in a different set of control experiments where cells expressing only CENP-A-GFP without SiR-tubulin were imaged with the same illumination protocol (Figure 2D,G,H; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B,D,E).
evidence: The manuscript reports control experiments showing specificity of the observed effects.

claim: The observed effects in opto cells were not a consequence of SiR-tubulin or laser photodamage.
source: Therefore, the observed effects in opto cells were not a consequence of SiR-tubulin or laser photodamage (Douthwright and Sluder, 2017).
evidence: The manuscript draws a conclusion based on control experiments and cites a reference about photodamage.

claim: In contrast to acute removal, long-term depletion of PRC1 by siRNA did not cause kinetochore misalignment or misorientation.
source: Strikingly, in contrast to acute removal, the long-term depletion did not cause kinetochore misalignment or misorientation (Figure 2D,H; Figure 2—figure supplement 1H,I; Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative comparisons between acute and long-term PRC1 depletion effects.

claim: Acute and long-term PRC1 removal decreased the inter-kinetochore distance to a similar extent.
source: The two methods decreased the inter-kinetochore distance to a similar extent (Figure 2G; Figure 2—figure supplement 1J; Table 1)
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative comparisons of inter-kinetochore distance changes between acute and long-term PRC1 depletion.

claim: Long-term PRC1 depletion reduced the fraction of cells that entered anaphase.
source: even though unlike acute removal, long-term removal reduced the fraction of cells that entered anaphase (35 ± 8%, N = 37, and 79 ± 6%, N = 37, for PRC1 siRNA treated and untreated, respectively; p = 0.046, Pearson's Chi-squared test; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative data comparing anaphase entry rates with statistical analysis.

claim: Acute removal of PRC1 results in different effects in comparison with long-term depletion.
source: Thus, acute removal of PRC1 results in different effects in comparison with a long-term depletion.
evidence: The manuscript draws a conclusion based on comparing effects of acute and long-term PRC1 depletion.

claim: Lagging kinetochores occurred more frequently when opto-PRC1 was being removed than in control cells.
source: We found that lagging kinetochores occurred more frequently when opto-PRC1 was being removed than in control cells (Figure 2I,J; Figure 2—video 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative data comparing lagging kinetochore frequency with reference to figures and videos.

claim: Long-term depletion of PRC1 by siRNA increased the frequency of lagging kinetochores during early anaphase.
source: Similarly, long-term depletion of PRC1 by siRNA also increased the frequency of lagging kinetochores during early anaphase (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A; Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative data on lagging kinetochore frequency after long-term PRC1 depletion.

claim: Opto cells that showed lagging kinetochores in anaphase had a slightly smaller inter-kinetochore distance before anaphase than opto cells without lagging kinetochores.
source: Opto cells that showed lagging kinetochores in anaphase had a slightly smaller inter-kinetochore distance before anaphase than opto cells without lagging kinetochores (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B), suggesting that a decrease in tension may be involved in the imperfect kinetochore segregation.
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative measurements comparing inter-kinetochore distances between cells with and without lagging kinetochores.

claim: Misalignment and lagging kinetochores are not linked on the cell level, although they may be linked locally on individual kinetochores.
source: The cells with lagging kinetochores did not have a larger average kinetochore misalignment in metaphase (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C), which indicates that misalignment and lagging kinetochores are not linked on the cell level, although they may be linked locally on individual kinetochores.
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative data and draws conclusions about the relationship between misalignment and lagging kinetochores.

claim: CLASP1 did not accumulate between segregating chromosomes in opto HeLa cells stably expressing EGFP-CLASP1.
source: As perturbation of the PRC1-CLASP1 interaction and the consequent absence of CLASP1 from the spindle midzone results in lagging chromosomes (Liu et al., 2009), we inspected the localization of CLASP1 and found that it did not accumulate between segregating chromosomes in opto HeLa cells stably expressing EGFP-CLASP1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The manuscript reports observations of CLASP1 localization with reference to a figure and cites published work.

claim: The observed higher occurrence of lagging kinetochores could be attributed to changes in tension during metaphase, perturbed recruitment of CLASP1 to the spindle midzone by PRC1 during early anaphase, or a combination of both effects.
source: Thus, the observed higher occurrence of lagging kinetochores could be attributed to changes in tension during metaphase, perturbed recruitment of CLASP1 to the spindle midzone by PRC1 during early anaphase, or a combination of both effects.
evidence: The manuscript proposes multiple possible mechanistic explanations for the observed lagging kinetochore phenotype.

claim: Acute PRC1 removal leads to chromosome misalignment and elongation of overlap zones.
source: Our finding that acute PRC1 removal leads to chromosome misalignment and elongation of overlap zones supports this model.
evidence: The manuscript states that experimental findings support their proposed model.

claim: Elongation of overlaps correlates with chromosome misalignment within spindles.
source: Moreover, elongation of overlaps correlates with chromosome misalignment within spindles, as elongated overlaps and misaligned chromosomes are mostly found in the central part of the spindle rather than on the periphery.
evidence: The manuscript reports a spatial correlation between overlap elongation and chromosome misalignment.

claim: Long-term PRC1 depletion by siRNA leads neither to overlap elongation nor chromosome misalignment.
source: In contrast to the acute PRC1 removal, long-term PRC1 depletion by siRNA leads neither to overlap elongation nor chromosome misalignment, providing further support to our model.
evidence: The manuscript reports differences between acute and long-term PRC1 depletion effects.

claim: There exist compensatory mechanisms that regulate overlap length and maintain chromosome alignment during long-term PRC1 depletion.
source: These differences between the acute and long-term depletion indicate the existence of compensatory mechanisms that regulate overlap length and hence maintain chromosome alignment during long-term PRC1 depletion.
evidence: The manuscript infers the existence of compensatory mechanisms based on differences between acute and long-term depletion.

claim: Kif4A and Kif18A localize in the bridging fibers in metaphase.
source: Interestingly, we found that Kif4A and Kif18A localize in the bridging fibers in metaphase and their intensities decreased following partial disassembly of the bridging fiber by optogenetic or siRNA-mediated PRC1 removal.
evidence: The manuscript reports observations of protein localization with reference to figures.

claim: Kif4A and Kif18A suppress microtubule dynamics.
source: Both Kif4A and Kif18A suppress microtubule dynamics (Bieling et al., 2010b; Bringmann et al., 2004; Stumpff et al., 2008; Stumpff et al., 2012)
evidence: The manuscript cites published work about the functions of Kif4A and Kif18A.

claim: Depletion of Kif4A or Kif18A by siRNA leads to longer PRC1-labeled overlaps.
source: and our experiments showed that depletion of either of them by siRNA leads to longer PRC1-labeled overlaps.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results showing effects of Kif4A and Kif18A depletion on overlap length.

claim: Kif4A and Kif18A siRNA-treated cells exhibit chromosome misalignment.
source: These elongated PRC1-labeled overlaps provide another line of evidence in support of our model for chromosome alignment by overlap length-dependent forces, as Kif4A and Kif18A siRNA-treated cells exhibit chromosome misalignment (Stumpff et al., 2008; Wandke et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites published work showing chromosome misalignment after Kif4A and Kif18A depletion.

claim: There is a small pool of Kif4A that binds to the antiparallel overlaps of bridging microtubules in metaphase.
source: Even though it was reported that Kif4A does not directly interact with PRC1 before late mitosis (Gruneberg et al., 2006; Kurasawa et al., 2004; Zhu and Jiang, 2005), our experiments suggest that there is a small pool of Kif4A that does so and binds to the antiparallel overlaps of bridging microtubules in metaphase.
evidence: The manuscript proposes a new finding that contrasts with published work, based on experimental observations.

claim: Acute PRC1 removal results in the removal of a pool of Kif4A from the bridge.
source: Acute PRC1 removal likely results in the removal of this pool of Kif4A from the bridge.
evidence: The manuscript infers a consequence of PRC1 removal based on observed Kif4A localization changes.

claim: Kif4A was reduced by ~76% within 12 min of acute PRC1 removal, which is similar to the reduction of PRC1 by ~85% within the same time interval.
source: Our result that Kif4A was reduced by ~76%, which is similar to the reduction of PRC1 by ~85% within the same time interval (12 min) of acute removal supports this picture.
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative measurements comparing Kif4A and PRC1 reduction kinetics.

claim: The reduction of Kif4A in the bridge may lead to excessive microtubule polymerization and thus longer overlap zones in metaphase.
source: This reduction of Kif4A in the bridge may lead to excessive microtubule polymerization and thus longer overlap zones in metaphase, similar to the long overlaps in anaphase after Kif4A depletion (Hu et al., 2011; Kurasawa et al., 2004; Zhu and Jiang, 2005).
evidence: The manuscript proposes a mechanistic explanation based on experimental observations and cites published work.

claim: The spindle length remained constant after acute PRC1 removal.
source: As the spindle length remained constant after acute PRC1 removal, we suggest that the overlap elongation is due to Kif4A acting specifically on bridging microtubules rather than overall spindle microtubules.
evidence: The manuscript reports an observation and draws a conclusion about the specificity of Kif4A action.

claim: Kif18A in the bridging fiber was reduced less than PRC1 within 12 min of acute PRC1 removal, ~43% compared with ~85%, respectively.
source: In contrast to Kif4A, Kif18A in the bridging fiber was reduced less than PRC1 within 12 min of acute PRC1 removal, ~43% compared with ~85%, respectively.
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative measurements comparing Kif18A and PRC1 reduction kinetics.

claim: The reduction of Kif18A in the bridge was a consequence of the fewer microtubules in the bridging fiber, and the amount of Kif18A per microtubule remained largely unaffected by PRC1 removal.
source: This difference in the behavior of Kif18A and PRC1 is consistent with the fact that Kif18A is not known to be a binding partner of PRC1. Thus, we infer that the reduction of Kif18A in the bridge was a consequence of the fewer microtubules in the bridging fiber, and that the amount of Kif18A per microtubule remained largely unaffected by PRC1 removal.
evidence: The manuscript draws conclusions about Kif18A behavior based on quantitative data and known protein interactions.

claim: MKLP1 was reduced to a similar extent as PRC1, ~87% and ~88% within 20 min of acute PRC1 removal, respectively.
source: Finally, MKLP1, which is a binding partner of PRC1 (Gruneberg et al., 2006), was reduced to a similar extent as PRC1, ~87% and ~88% within 20 min of acute PRC1 removal, respectively.
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative measurements comparing MKLP1 and PRC1 reduction kinetics and cites published work about their interaction.

claim: The localization of MKLP1 and a small pool of Kif4A in the bridging fiber are directly PRC1-dependent, whereas the localization of Kif18A is not.
source: Based on these results, we conclude that the localization of MKLP1 and a small pool of Kif4A in the bridging fiber are directly PRC1-dependent, whereas the localization of Kif18A is not.
evidence: The manuscript draws conclusions about protein localization dependencies based on quantitative data.

claim: Both Kif4A and Kif18A regulate the length of bridging microtubules and their overlaps under normal conditions.
source: We propose that both Kif4A and Kif18A regulate the length of bridging microtubules and their overlaps under normal conditions (Figure 6C), as their depletion results in longer overlaps.
evidence: The manuscript proposes a model based on experimental observations of overlap length changes after Kif4A and Kif18A depletion.

claim: Kif4A signal in the bridging fibers decreased to a larger extent after acute than after long-term PRC1 depletion.
source: Intriguingly, we found that Kif4A signal in the bridging fibers decreased to a larger extent after acute than after long-term PRC1 depletion, whereas Kif18A signal decreased to a similar extent by the two methods of PRC1 depletion.
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative comparisons of Kif4A and Kif18A signal changes between acute and long-term PRC1 depletion.

claim: Kif4A depletion by siRNA resulted in an increase of ~1 µm in overlap length, which was similar to the increase observed after acute PRC1 removal.
source: Moreover, Kif4A depletion by siRNA resulted in an increase of ~1 µm in overlap length, which was similar to the increase observed after acute PRC1 removal, whereas Kif18A depletion by siRNA led to a larger overlap increase.
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative measurements comparing overlap length changes after different treatments.

claim: The observed overlap elongation after acute PRC1 removal is a consequence of the strong reduction of Kif4A in the bridging fibers.
source: Thus, we suggest that the observed overlap elongation after acute PRC1 removal is a consequence of the strong reduction of Kif4A in the bridging fibers.
evidence: The manuscript proposes a mechanistic explanation based on quantitative data.

claim: After long-term PRC1 depletion, a larger fraction of Kif4A is present on the microtubules during overlap formation, contributing to the compensatory mechanism maintaining normal overlap length.
source: In contrast, after long-term PRC1 depletion, we speculate that a larger fraction of Kif4A is present on the microtubules during overlap formation, contributing to the compensatory mechanism maintaining normal overlap length.
evidence: The manuscript proposes a speculative explanation for differences between acute and long-term PRC1 depletion.

claim: Kif4A and Eg5 may slide apart bridging microtubules during metaphase.
source: The proteins that we found in the bridging fiber, Kif4A, Kif18A, and MKLP1, may also slide apart and/or stabilize the bridging microtubules (Figure 6C). In addition to these kinesins, we observed Eg5 in the bridging fiber (Kajtez et al., 2016; Mann and Wadsworth, 2018). During early anaphase, Kif4A and Eg5 drive the sliding of antiparallel microtubules that elongates the spindle (Vukušić et al., 2019). Thus, these kinesins may have a similar role during metaphase.
evidence: The manuscript proposes a function based on observations and cites published work about protein localization and function in anaphase.

claim: Kif4A depletion reduces microtubule poleward flux in metaphase.
source: This possibility is in agreement with previous work showing that Kif4A depletion reduces microtubule poleward flux in metaphase (Wandke et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites published work supporting their proposed model.

claim: Kif18A in the bridging fiber may have microtubule sliding and crosslinking activities equivalent to those of the yeast kinesin-8.
source: Similarly, Kif18A in the bridging fiber may have microtubule sliding and crosslinking activities equivalent to those of the yeast kinesin-8 (Su et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript proposes a function based on analogy to published work on yeast kinesin-8.

claim: MKLP1 contributes to the stabilization of bridging microtubules in early anaphase.
source: Furthermore, MKLP1 contributes to the stabilization of bridging microtubules in early anaphase (Vukušić et al., 2017), and we suggest that it performs a similar function in metaphase together with other motors and crosslinkers including Eg5 and PRC1.
evidence: The manuscript cites published work and proposes an extension of the function to metaphase.

claim: The localization of Kif4A on chromosome arms was preserved after acute PRC1 removal.
source: The localization of Kif4A on chromosome arms, where it is involved in polar ejection forces (Bieling et al., 2010a; Brouhard and Hunt, 2005) was preserved after acute PRC1 removal.
evidence: The manuscript reports observations of Kif4A localization and cites published work about its function.

claim: Kif18A, CLASP1, and CENP-E remained on plus-ends of k-fibers after acute PRC1 removal.
source: Similarly, Kif18A, CLASP1, and CENP-E remained on plus-ends of k-fibers.
evidence: The manuscript reports observations of protein localization after PRC1 removal.

claim: The observed chromosome misalignment and overlap elongation after acute PRC1 removal could also be promoted by changes of the dynamics of other microtubules within the spindle.
source: However, as we cannot exclude potential subtle changes in the localization of these proteins or mislocalization of other proteins, the observed chromosome misalignment and overlap elongation after acute PRC1 removal could also be promoted by the changes of the dynamics of other microtubules within the spindle consequently affecting forces produced by k-fibers and polar ejection forces.
evidence: The manuscript acknowledges alternative explanations for the observed phenotypes.

claim: The most affected part of the spindle upon acute PRC1 removal was the inner part, where the PRC1 signal disappeared faster and the bridging microtubules became longer than on the periphery.
source: The changes upon acute PRC1 removal were not spatially uniform across the spindle. The most affected part was the inner part of the spindle, where the PRC1 signal disappeared faster and the bridging microtubules became longer than on the periphery of the spindle.
evidence: The manuscript reports spatial differences in the effects of PRC1 removal.

claim: The inner bridging fibers were more severely affected by PRC1 removal possibly because they are made up of fewer microtubules than the outer bridges.
source: The inner bridging fibers were more severely affected by PRC1 removal possibly because they are made up of fewer microtubules than the outer bridges.
evidence: The manuscript proposes an explanation for spatial differences in PRC1 removal effects.

claim: Severely misaligned kinetochores and lagging kinetochores occurred more often in the inner part of the spindle.
source: Severely misaligned kinetochores that moved more than 2 µm away from the equatorial plane and lagging kinetochores occurred also more often in the inner part of the spindle.
evidence: The manuscript reports spatial distribution of misaligned and lagging kinetochores.

claim: The local effect of PRC1 removal is in line with weak mechanical coupling between neighboring k-fibers yet strong coupling between sister k-fibers.
source: This local effect is in line with weak mechanical coupling between neighboring k-fibers yet strong coupling between sister k-fibers (Elting et al., 2017; Suresh et al., 2020; Vladimirou et al., 2013), and indicative of a mechanistic link between the bridging fiber geometry and kinetochore alignment.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the spatial effects in the context of published work on k-fiber coupling.

claim: Overlap length-dependent forces help to position the chromosomes at the equatorial plane of the spindle.
source: In conclusion, we propose that overlap length-dependent forces help to position the chromosomes at the equatorial plane of the spindle.
evidence: The manuscript proposes a model based on experimental findings.

claim: The overlap length is regulated by the PRC1-dependent Kif4A, and by Kif18A within the bridging fiber.
source: The overlap length is regulated by the PRC1-dependent Kif4A, and by Kif18A within the bridging fiber.
evidence: The manuscript proposes a regulatory mechanism based on experimental findings.

claim: Kif4A, Eg5, and possibly other kinesins may slide bridging microtubules apart, whereas PRC1 together with the kinesins stabilizes the overlaps.
source: Kif4A, Eg5, and possibly other kinesins may slide bridging microtubules apart, whereas PRC1 together with the kinesins stabilizes the overlaps.
evidence: The manuscript proposes a mechanistic model for bridging fiber regulation.

claim: Proper chromosome alignment requires forces generated within the bridging fiber, which are transferred to the k-fiber and rely on precise regulation of the overlap region.
source: Thus, in addition to the forces generated at k-fiber tips and polar ejection forces, proper chromosome alignment requires forces generated within the bridging fiber, which are transferred to the k-fiber and rely on precise regulation of the overlap region.
evidence: The manuscript proposes a comprehensive model integrating multiple force-generating mechanisms.

claim: 88 ± 3% of opto-PRC1 was removed after 20 min of exposure to blue light.
source: We found that 88 ± 3% of opto-PRC1 was removed after 20 min of exposure to the blue light with a half-time of 4.2 ± 0.1 min (Figure 1C).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative data with reference to Figure 1C showing the removal kinetics.

claim: 1.8 ± 0.2 EB3 spots per minute per bridging fiber were observed in control cells.
source: We found 1.8 ± 0.2 EB3 spots per minute per bridging fiber in control cells, showing that bridging fibers are dynamically remodeled during metaphase (Figure 3D).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative data with reference to Figure 3D showing EB3 spot frequency.

claim: The number of EB3 spots was similar after opto-PRC1 removal, 2.0 ± 0.3 spots/min.
source: This number was similar after opto-PRC1 removal, 2.0 ± 0.3 spots/min (p = 0.59; t-test, Figure 3D), suggesting that the number of dynamic microtubules in the bridge is largely unaffected by acute PRC1 removal.
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative data with statistical analysis and reference to Figure 3D.

claim: In PRC1 siRNA-treated cells, 1.5 ± 0.1 EB3 spots/min were observed compared to 1.91 ± 0.09 spots/min in untreated cells.
source: However, in PRC1 siRNA-treated cells fewer EB3 spots were observed to move to opposite spindle half, 1.5 ± 0.1 EB3 spots/min, compared to untreated cells, where 1.91 ± 0.09 spots/min were observed (p = 0.01; t-test, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), indicating that long-term PRC1 depletion slightly decreases the number of dynamic microtubules in the bridge.
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative data with statistical analysis and reference to a supplementary figure.

claim: In control cells, the overlap half-length was 1.8 ± 0.2 µm.
source: In control cell, the overlap half-length was 1.8 ± 0.2 µm (n = 17 spots in N = 9 cells; Figure 3G, right), which corresponds well to the overlap half-length measured as the half-length of PRC1 streaks in this cell line, 0.5x(3.8 ± 0.4) µm (N = 9 cells; Figure 3H), validating our method for overlap length measurement based on EB3 tracks.
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative measurements with reference to figures and validates the measurement method.

claim: After opto-PRC1 removal, the overlap half-length increased to 2.6 ± 0.2 µm.
source: After opto-PRC1 removal, the overlap half-length increased to 2.6 ± 0.2 µm (n = 23 spots in N = 9 cells; Figure 3G).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative measurements with reference to a figure.

claim: Treatment with PRC1 siRNA did not result in a change of overlap length with respect to untreated cells.
source: In contrast to opto cells, treatment with PRC1 siRNA did not result in a change of overlap length with respect to untreated cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: The manuscript reports no significant change in overlap length after long-term PRC1 depletion with reference to supplementary figures.

claim: The antiparallel overlaps became on average 40% longer after acute PRC1 removal.
source: Thus, the antiparallel overlaps became on average 40% longer after acute, but unchanged after long-time PRC1 removal.
evidence: The manuscript provides a quantitative summary of overlap length changes comparing acute and long-term PRC1 removal.

claim: Upon exposure to blue light, tubulin signal intensity in the bridging fibers decreased ~2.5-fold, which corresponds to 5.6 ± 0.9 microtubules.
source: Upon exposure to the blue light, tubulin signal intensity in the bridging fibers decreased ~2.5-fold, which corresponds to 5.6 ± 0.9 microtubules given that the average number of microtubules in the bridging fiber is 14 (Kajtez et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative measurements of microtubule number changes and cites published work for the baseline number.

claim: In the presence of PRC1, the bridge contains more microtubules with a smaller fraction of them being dynamic than without PRC1.
source: Together with the finding that the number of growing microtubules in the bridging fiber is similar with and without PRC1 (Figure 3D), this result implies that in the presence of PRC1 the bridge contains more microtubules with a smaller fraction of them being dynamic than without PRC1, and that PRC1 removal leads mainly to disassembly of non-dynamic microtubules.
evidence: The manuscript draws conclusions about microtubule composition based on quantitative data from multiple figures.

claim: Long-term depletion of PRC1 by siRNA resulted in a decreased number of microtubules in the bridge, 7.5 ± 1.1, which was similar to the microtubule number after acute removal.
source: Long-term depletion resulted in a decreased number of microtubules in the bridge, 7.5 ± 1.1, which was similar to the microtubule number after acute removal (p = 0.21, t-test; Figure 4—figure supplement 1I, Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative measurements comparing microtubule numbers between acute and long-term PRC1 depletion with statistical analysis.

claim: PRC1 removal straightened the k-fibers and made the spindle diamond-shaped.
source: Tracking of the pole-to-pole contour of the outermost k-fibers revealed that PRC1 removal indeed straightened the k-fibers and thus made the spindle diamond-shaped (Figure 4—figure supplement 1K–M).
evidence: The manuscript reports observations of k-fiber shape changes with reference to supplementary figures.

claim: Long-term depletion of PRC1 caused straightening of outermost k-fibers, although to a smaller extent than acute removal.
source: Similar to acute removal, long-term depletion of PRC1 caused straightening of outermost k-fibers, although to a smaller extent, whereas spindle length and width were unchanged after both treatments (Figure 4—figure supplement 1L,N,O; Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative comparisons of k-fiber curvature changes between acute and long-term PRC1 depletion.

claim: Eg5/kinesin-5 was still detectable in bridging fibers after PRC1 siRNA.
source: Since bridging fibers are, nevertheless, present upon PRC1 removal, we asked how the residual microtubules are bundled together. Eg5/kinesin-5, which localizes in the bridging fibers (Kajtez et al., 2016; Mann and Wadsworth, 2018), was still detectable in these fibers after PRC1 siRNA (Figure 4—figure supplement 1P).
evidence: The manuscript reports observations of Eg5 localization after PRC1 depletion with reference to a supplementary figure and cites published work.

claim: Kif4A and Kif18A localize in the bridge during metaphase in a PRC1-dependent manner.
source: Kif4A/kinesin-4 and Kif18A/kinesin-8 were found within the bridging fiber and largely lost upon PRC1 removal, suggesting that these proteins regulate the overlap length of bridging microtubules.
evidence: The manuscript reports observations of protein localization and changes upon PRC1 removal.

claim: PRC1 removal did not affect the localization of Kif4A on the chromosomes and Kif18A, CLASP1, and CENP-E/kinesin-7 on the plus ends of k-fibers.
source: PRC1 removal did not affect the localization of Kif4A on the chromosomes and Kif18A, CLASP1, and CENP-E/kinesin-7 on the plus ends of k-fibers, arguing against perturbed polar ejection forces or molecular events at the kinetochore microtubule plus ends as origins of the observed kinetochore misalignment.
evidence: The manuscript reports observations of protein localization after PRC1 removal and draws conclusions about the mechanism of kinetochore misalignment.

claim: Bridging microtubules buffer chromosome movements, thus promoting their alignment.
source: In conclusion, our optogenetic experiments show that bridging microtubules buffer chromosome movements, thus promoting their alignment.
evidence: The manuscript draws a conclusion based on the overall experimental findings.

claim: Chromosome alignment occurs via length-dependent forces, which depend on the antiparallel overlap length within the bridging fiber.
source: We propose that this occurs via length-dependent forces, which depend on the antiparallel overlap length within the bridging fiber.
evidence: The manuscript proposes a mechanistic model based on experimental findings.
